column4: One candlestick tells a whole story. In a single shape it captures a period's battle between buyers and sellers, who pushed harder, and where price finally settled. Learn to read one candle and a chart stops looking like noise. In the next few minutes you'll break a candle down to its parts, tell a bullish one from a bearish one, judge the pressure behind it, and see why the same stock can look completely different depending on the timeframe you view.

Start with the anatomy. Look at the candle drawn on screen. The thick middle part is the body, and it spans the open and the close, the first and last price of the period. The thin lines above and below are the wicks, sometimes called shadows, and they reach up to the high and down to the low. So one candle packs four prices into a single shape: open, high, low, and close. A plain line chart would give you only the close. The candle shows you the full range and the fight inside it. Picture it as one round of a tug-of-war between buyers and sellers.

Color tells you who won. A green or white body means the close finished above the open, so buyers were in control that period. A red or black body means the close finished below the open, so sellers took over. Size matters too. A long body signals strong, one-sided pressure, an intense battle with a clear winner. A short body means the open and close landed close together, low volatility, a balanced fight with no decisive result.

Now zoom out and back in. The same stock looks different depending on the timeframe. On the mountain image, the weekly view shows the whole range, the daily shows the middle ground, and the hourly zooms into fine detail. Each chart is the same mountain seen from a different distance. Traders use more than one timeframe on purpose. A signal on the hourly chart carries more weight when the daily and weekly agree with it. That's multiple-timeframe analysis, checking a short-term move against the broader context.

Your turn to build one. Drag the open and close sliders and watch the candle redraw. When you set the close above the open, the body turns green and the verdict reads bullish, buyers won. Drop the close below the open and it flips red, bearish, sellers won. Line them up exactly and you get a doji, a standoff with no clear winner. These values are illustrative, just a way to feel how the open and the close decide the color and the story.

Let's put it together. Sort each card into bullish or bearish. Tap a card to pick it up, then tap the column where it belongs. Ask one question each time: did buyers or sellers finish in control? A green body, a run of higher closes, a long lower wick where buyers defended a dip, those lean bullish. A red body, lower closes, a long upper wick where sellers rejected the highs, those lean bearish.
Five quick questions to lock it in. Answer them to earn your points for the lesson.

Carry these with you. A candle's body runs from open to close, and its wicks reach the high and low. Green means buyers won the period, red means sellers did, and a longer body means a stronger push. And the same stock reads differently across timeframes, so confirm a signal on more than one. Next up we build on this: support, resistance, trend, and volume, the levels and forces that tell you where candles are likely to turn.
